lead: A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) says the data comes from several Gaussian bells added together with weights. Each bell is a component with its own mean and covariance. The hidden part is which component produced each point. The EM algorithm estimates those hidden memberships and the component parameters together. GMMs are used for soft clustering, density estimation, speaker recognition and anomaly detection. They fit blobs of different shapes and sizes, which k-means cannot do.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for clustering, Unit 1 for probability distributions, and Unit 3 for Bayes and maximum likelihood.

blocks.text: A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) writes the probability density of a point x as a weighted sum of K Gaussian densities. The weights are called mixing weights. Each Gaussian is one component of the mixture.
p(x) = Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>K</sup> π<sub>k</sub> N(x | μ<sub>k</sub>, Σ<sub>k</sub>)
blocks.where: K is the number of components; π<sub>k</sub> is the mixing weight of component k, with π<sub>k</sub> ≥ 0 and Σ<sub>k</sub> π<sub>k</sub> = 1; μ<sub>k</sub> is its mean vector; Σ<sub>k</sub> is its covariance matrix; N is the Gaussian density.

blocks.text: N(x | μ, Σ) = 1 / ((2π)<sup>d/2</sup> |Σ|<sup>1/2</sup>) × exp(−½ (x − μ)<sup>T</sup> Σ<sup>−1</sup> (x − μ))
blocks.where: d is the number of features; |Σ| is the determinant of the covariance matrix; Σ<sup>−1</sup> is its inverse; (x − μ)<sup>T</sup> is the transpose of the vector x − μ.

blocks.text: The model has a generative story. First pick component k with probability π<sub>k</sub>. Then draw x from that component's Gaussian. The component label z<sub>i</sub> is hidden. You see x<sub>i</sub> only. The label z<sub>i</sub> takes one value from 1 to K but is not in the data.

Because each component has its own covariance matrix, a GMM can fit elongated, tilted and overlapping blobs. A single Gaussian cannot. K-means, covered in Chapter 4.2, uses hard round-ish clusters instead.

EM treats the hidden labels as missing data. It repeats two steps from an initial θ = (π, μ, Σ). The E-step computes each point's responsibility: the probability that component k produced point i, given the current parameters.
r<sub>ik</sub> = π<sub>k</sub> N(x<sub>i</sub> | μ<sub>k</sub>, Σ<sub>k</sub>) ÷ Σ<sub>j=1</sub><sup>K</sup> π<sub>j</sub> N(x<sub>i</sub> | μ<sub>j</sub>, Σ<sub>j</sub>)
blocks.where: r<sub>ik</sub> is the responsibility of component k for point i; for each point i, the responsibilities over all k sum to 1.

items: Initialise π, μ and Σ for all K components. Random values or a k-means result both work.
E-step: compute r<sub>ik</sub> for every point i and component k from the current parameters.

M-step: update the parameters using the responsibilities as soft counts: π<sub>k</sub> = (1/n) Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> r<sub>ik</sub>, the average responsibility of component k; μ<sub>k</sub> = Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> r<sub>ik</sub> x<sub>i</sub> ÷ Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> r<sub>ik</sub>, a responsibility-weighted mean; Σ<sub>k</sub> = Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> r<sub>ik</sub> (x<sub>i</sub> − μ<sub>k</sub>)(x<sub>i</sub> − μ<sub>k</sub>)<sup>T</sup> ÷ Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> r<sub>ik</sub>, a responsibility-weighted covariance.
Compute the log-likelihood. Stop if it changes by less than a small threshold; otherwise go back to the E-step.

blocks.text: L(θ) = Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> log( Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>K</sup> π<sub>k</sub> N(x<sub>i</sub> | μ<sub>k</sub>, Σ<sub>k</sub>) )
blocks.where: L(θ) is the log-likelihood of the observed data under parameters θ; n is the number of points. EM never decreases L at an iteration.

blocks.text: K-means gives each point one hard label: the nearest centroid. A GMM gives each point a probability in every component. That is a soft assignment. If you need a hard cluster after EM, take the component with the largest responsibility for each point.

GMMs are more flexible than k-means. Components can have different weights, different spreads and tilted covariance shapes. K-means tends to split round, similar-sized clusters and can struggle when clusters overlap. When all components share one spherical covariance and equal weights, EM behaves much like soft k-means.

items: A GMM is a probabilistic model, so it also gives a density value p(x). K-means gives only cluster labels.
Fuzzy clustering in Chapter 4.9 also uses memberships, but its memberships are not probabilities from a Gaussian model.
Evaluation of the final clusters is a separate step; see Chapter 4.8.

figure.caption: EM cycles between computing responsibilities and updating the mixture parameters. The loop stops when the log-likelihood changes little, and the output is a soft cluster assignment.

spec.title: EM cycle
spec.aria: EM starts with parameters θ, repeats an E-step for responsibilities and an M-step for parameters until convergence, then outputs soft clusters.

examples.question: Three one-dimensional points are x = 0, 1, 4. Fit a two-component GMM with equal weights π<sub>1</sub> = π<sub>2</sub> = 0.5 and with the variances fixed at σ<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> = σ<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> = 1. Initial means are μ<sub>1</sub> = 0 and μ<sub>2</sub> = 4. Do one E-step and one M-step for the means. Give the responsibilities for component 1 and the updated means.
steps: Use the one-dimensional Gaussian N(x | μ, 1) = (1/√(2π)) exp(−(x − μ)²/2). The constant 1/√(2π) cancels in every responsibility because the weights are equal.
examples.answer: The component-1 responsibilities are about 0.9997, 0.9820 and 0.0003 for x = 0, 1, 4. The updated means are μ<sub>1</sub> ≈ 0.4961 and μ<sub>2</sub> ≈ 3.9457.
examples.check:
import math
xs = [0, 1, 4]
def g(x, m):
    return math.exp(-((x - m) ** 2) / 2)
r = [g(x, 0) / (g(x, 0) + g(x, 4)) for x in xs]
for v in r:
    print(f'{v:.4f}')
s = sum(r)
mu1 = sum(ri * x for ri, x in zip(r, xs)) / s
print(f'{mu1:.4f}')
s2 = sum(1 - ri for ri in r)
mu2 = sum((1 - ri) * x for ri, x in zip(r, xs)) / s2
print(f'{mu2:.4f}')

traps: Responsibilities r<sub>ik</sub> are probabilities that sum to 1 over components for each point. They are not hard labels; use argmax only after EM if a hard cluster is needed.
EM increases the likelihood from the current start. It can stop at a local optimum, so run several initialisations and keep the best final likelihood.
An unconstrained variance can collapse to zero when a component owns one point. Add a small value to the diagonal or use a prior/minimum variance.
Mixing weights π<sub>k</sub> are not the same as hard cluster sizes. They are model probabilities and must sum to 1.

quiz.q: What constraint do the mixing weights π<sub>k</sub> satisfy in a GMM?
Why is the component label z<sub>i</sub> called latent?
quiz.a: It is not observed. The model assumes each x<sub>i</sub> came from one component, but only x<sub>i</sub> is in the data.

quiz.q: For one point, π<sub>1</sub> = 0.5, N(x | μ<sub>1</sub>, Σ<sub>1</sub>) = 0.4, π<sub>2</sub> = 0.5 and N(x | μ<sub>2</sub>, Σ<sub>2</sub>) = 0.1. Find r<sub>1</sub>.
EM's log-likelihood never decreases, yet the final clustering can be poor. Explain both facts.
quiz.a: Each E-step and M-step increases or keeps the log-likelihood, so the sequence is non-decreasing. The sequence can reach a local maximum that depends on initial θ, so another start may give a better optimum.

quiz.q: Write the E-step responsibility formula for component k and point i.
quiz.a: r<sub>ik</sub> = π<sub>k</sub> N(x<sub>i</sub> | μ<sub>k</sub>, Σ<sub>k</sub>) / Σ<sub>j</sub> π<sub>j</sub> N(x<sub>i</sub> | μ<sub>j</sub>, Σ<sub>j</sub>).

quiz.q: Give one difference between GMM responsibilities and k-means assignment.
quiz.a: GMM gives a probability r<sub>ik</sub> in every component; k-means gives one hard label to the nearest centroid.

quiz.q: A one-dimensional GMM component ends up responsible for a single point and its variance goes to 0. What goes wrong and what is one fix?
quiz.a: The Gaussian becomes a spike and the likelihood can go to infinity; add a small positive value to the variance or use a prior/minimum variance.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, libraries such as scikit-learn provide GaussianMixture with multiple restarts and BIC for choosing K. GMMs appear in speaker diarisation, background subtraction in video, and anomaly scores from density values. Research moves to Bayesian GMMs and variational inference, which avoid singularities and estimate K. Hidden Markov models stack GMM emissions for speech. Search for Gaussian mixture model scikit-learn, BIC model selection, and variational Gaussian mixture.
